facts.text: This is the New York Times customer care desk. Mia contacts them about her All Access subscription.

evidence.quote: Hello NYTimes Customer Care,

facts.text: In May 2025 Mia's introductory rate ended and she was charged $25.00 on May 3, 2025. She asked them to cancel and refund that charge as a one-time exception.

evidence.quote: I was charged $25.00 on May 3, 2025
refund the May 3 charge of $25.00 as a one-time exception

facts.text: In 2025, Mia said she had not used articles, Games or Cooking since early April.

evidence.quote: I have not read any articles or used the Games or Cooking apps

facts.text: Mia finished the May 2025 cancellation herself by following their link, and replied with one word.

evidence.quote: done

facts.text: Mia subscribed again in November 2025 at the $1 per week introductory rate. In January 2026 the rate changed to $25.00 every four weeks without her noticing.

evidence.quote: I subscribed at the $1 per week introductory rate in November 2025

facts.text: Mia was charged $25.00 on January 10, February 7, March 7 and April 4, 2026, $100.00 in total. She has not logged in since December 2025.

evidence.quote: for a total of $100.00
I have not logged in since December 2025.

facts.text: Mia wants refunds to go to the original payment method, not account credits. If first-level support cannot approve a refund, she asks them to escalate it.

evidence.quote: to the original payment method rather than account credits
please escalate the request

facts.text: In April 2026 they cancelled the subscription and refunded the April 4 payment.

evidence.quote: Thanks for cancelling the subscription and refunding the April 4 payment.

facts.text: Still open (April 2026): Mia asked for a review of the remaining $75.00 (January 10 to March 7, 2026). She asked for a copy of the December rate-change notice, which she cannot find, or a refund.

evidence.quote: which total $75.00
Could you please send me a copy of that notice, or refund the remaining $75.00?
